introduction-the-digital-hoarding-proble.core: Cloud waste piles up from 'just in case' provisioning and forgotten resources: idle instances, unattached volumes, old snapshots, oversized machines. Typically 20–30% of spend is waste.

first_principles.problem: Nobody deletes anything because they might need it, and the bill grows with no added value.
truths: Creating resources is easy; cleaning up is forgotten.
derivation: **Use spot** even for some stateful work.
Make cleanup **systematic**, not a one-off sprint.

analogy.title: A storage unit you never visit
analogy.story: You pay every month for boxes you've forgotten you own.
analogy.breaks: Some 'idle' resources are DR standby, so verify before deleting.

example.title: A waste audit

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Big savings with zero functional change.

example.outcome: you can see waste for what it is.

check.q: Give two common types of cloud waste.
check.a: For example, unattached EBS volumes and idle or forgotten instances (also old snapshots and oversized resources).

rightsizing-the-recommender-system.core: Engineers provision for the worst imaginable peak. Rightsizing uses observed utilisation (CPU, memory, p95/p99) to recommend smaller or different instance types, sized for the real peak plus headroom.

first_principles.problem: A fleet averages 8% CPU because each instance was sized for a peak that never happens.
truths: Peaks can be handled by autoscaling rather than oversizing.

analogy.title: Buying a bus for a family of four
analogy.story: Just in case relatives visit, you drive a 40-seat bus every day. A car plus a rental for visits is far cheaper.
analogy.breaks: CPU averages hide bursts, so use percentiles and watch latency SLOs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Same SLOs at a fraction of the price.

points: Size to the peak plus headroom.

check.q: Why size to p95/p99 rather than average utilisation?
check.a: Averages hide bursts, and sizing to the average would cause saturation at peaks.

spot-orchestration-for-stateful-workload.core: Spot isn't only for stateless work. With checkpointing, replicated stateful sets, graceful drains on the 2-minute notice and fast reattachment of volumes, some stateful workloads (CI caches, Kafka consumers, ML training, some databases' replicas) can use spot safely.

first_principles.problem: Teams assume all stateful workloads need on-demand and miss 60–90% savings on tolerant ones.
truths: State can be checkpointed or replicated.
derivation: Put **replicas on spot**, primaries on on-demand.
**Handle the notice**: drain, flush, release leases.
**Diversify** instance pools; use the capacity-optimised strategy.

analogy.title: A relay team with backups
analogy.story: If a runner is pulled mid-race, the next one picks up the baton from the last checkpoint.
analogy.breaks: Single-primary databases with strict latency SLOs are still poor candidates.

example.title: ML training on spot

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Long jobs finish cheaply despite interruptions.

example.outcome: spot savings extend to resilient stateful workloads.

check.q: What makes ML training a good spot candidate despite being stateful?
check.a: Progress can be checkpointed regularly and resumed on a new instance after an interruption.

building-a-systematic-waste-reduction-pr.core: One-off cleanup sprints decay. A systematic programme automates detection (policies and scripts), assigns owners, sets SLAs for fixing, tracks waste as a KPI, and prevents waste with TTLs, auto-shutdown and guardrails.

first_principles.problem: After a big cleanup, waste returns to the same level within six months.
derivation: **Auto-remediate** safe cases (stop idle dev instances, delete old snapshots).
**Prevent**: TTL tags, schedules, guardrails; track a **waste %** KPI.

analogy.title: Regular housekeeping vs. spring cleaning
analogy.story: A daily tidy-up keeps the house clean; one annual deep clean doesn't.
analogy.breaks: Over-aggressive auto-deletion destroys needed resources, so warn first and keep backups.

example.title: A Cloud Custodian policy
example.scenario: Stop idle dev instances at night.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Dev compute runs about 60% fewer hours, automatically.

code.text:
policies:
  - name: stop-dev-offhours
    resource: ec2
    filters:
      - "tag:env": dev
      - type: offhour
        default_tz: utc
        offhour: 20
    actions: [stop]

check.q: Why do one-time cleanup sprints fail long term?
check.a: Waste is created continuously, so without automation and prevention it simply builds up again.
